physics = the science of matter, energy, force and motion
chemistry = the science of substances, their structure and how they react
molecular biology = the study of living things at the level of DNA, proteins and cells
astronomy = the scientific study of stars, planets and other objects in space
astrophysics = the branch of physics that explains how objects in space behave
genetics = the science of genes, heredity and variation in living things
biotechnology = the use of living cells or organisms to make products or solve problems
nanotechnology = engineering of materials and devices at an extremely small, atomic scale
robotics = the design and use of robots to do tasks
neuroscience = the scientific study of the brain and nervous system
microbiology = the study of microscopic organisms such as bacteria and viruses
biochemistry = the chemistry of processes inside living organisms
computer science = the study of computation, algorithms and how computers are designed and used
materials science = the study of the properties and uses of metals, plastics, ceramics and similar substances
quantum physics = the physics of the very small, where particles do not behave like everyday objects
nuclear physics = the physics of the nucleus of the atom, including fission and fusion
engineering = the practical use of science to design machines, structures and systems
applied science = scientific work aimed at solving a practical problem, not only at theory
life sciences = the group of sciences that study living organisms, including biology and medicine
theoretical research = scientific work based on models and reasoning rather than a new experiment
hypothesis = a testable idea that an experiment is designed to support or reject
peer review = checking a study by other experts before it is published
breakthrough = an important discovery or invention that changes what is possible
control group = the group in a study that does not receive the new treatment, used for comparison
double-blind study = a trial in which neither the patient nor the researcher knows who got the real treatment
research grant = money given to fund a scientific project, usually after a competition
scientific journal = a periodical that publishes research papers after expert checks
scholarly reference = a formal mention of another piece of research in a paper
methodology = the system of methods used in a particular study
replicate an experiment = to repeat a test to see if the same results appear
correlation = a statistical link between two things that does not by itself prove cause
causation = a relationship in which one thing actually makes another happen
statistical significance = a measure of whether a result is likely to be a real effect, not chance
sample size = the number of people or items included in a study
field research = research done outside the laboratory, in the real environment
prototype = the first working model of a new machine or product
patent = a legal right that stops others copying an invention for a limited time
technology transfer = moving an invention from a laboratory into commercial or public use
research ethics = rules that protect people, animals and honesty in scientific work
animal testing = using animals in experiments, especially to check safety of drugs or products
evidence-based = based on systematic research rather than opinion or tradition
scientific community = researchers as a group who share methods, journals and criticism
variable = a factor that can change in an experiment and may affect the result
finding = a result or conclusion that comes out of a study
groundbreaking = so new that it changes a field of study or practice
cutting-edge = using the newest ideas or technology in a field
state-of-the-art = the best and most modern available at the present time
innovation = a new idea, method or product that is put into use
pioneer = a person who is among the first to develop a new idea or method
obsolete = no longer used because something newer and better exists
trial and error = learning by trying different methods until one works
broadband = a fast, always-on internet connection to a home, school or office
encryption = turning data into a code so that only authorised people can read it
algorithm = a set of rules a computer follows to solve a problem or make a decision
cybersecurity = protecting computers, networks and data from attack or unauthorised access
digital footprint = the trail of data you leave through online activity
cloud computing = using remote servers on the internet to store data and run programs
database = an organised collection of information that a computer can search quickly
user interface = the screens, buttons and menus through which a person controls a program
bandwidth = the amount of data that can be sent over a connection in a given time
fibre-optic cable = a cable that carries data as pulses of light
firewall = software or hardware that blocks unauthorised traffic in or out of a network
two-factor authentication = a login method that needs a password plus a second check, such as a code on a phone
malware = software designed to damage a device or steal data
ransomware = malware that locks files and demands money to unlock them
data breach = an incident in which private information is copied or seen without permission
computer virus = harmful software that copies itself and can damage files or steal data
phishing = tricking someone into giving passwords or money through a fake message or site
operating system = the main software that runs a computer and other programs
programming language = a formal language used to write instructions for a computer
source code = the human-readable instructions that make up a program
open source = software whose code can be viewed, changed and shared by others
software update = a new version of a program that fixes problems or adds features
server = a computer that stores data or runs services for other computers
wireless network = a network that connects devices without cables, usually by radio
microchip = a tiny electronic circuit that processes or stores information
semiconductor = a material used to make chips, able to conduct electricity under some conditions
cloud storage = keeping files on remote internet servers rather than only on your own device
system outage = a period when a computer service is unavailable
video streaming = watching video over the internet without downloading the whole file first
search algorithm = the set of rules a search engine uses to rank pages
browser extension = a small add-on that changes how a web browser works
cookies = small files a site stores on your device to remember you or track visits
user agreement = the legal rules you accept when you use a digital service
digital exclusion = being left out of work or study because of poor access to digital technology
e-waste = discarded electronic devices that can leak toxic materials if dumped
coding = writing instructions that a computer can follow
processor speed = how quickly a computer’s central chip can carry out instructions
Bluetooth connection = a short-range wireless link between nearby devices
GPS tracking = using satellite signals to follow the location of a person or object
artificial intelligence = computer systems that perform tasks that usually need human thinking
machine learning = a method in which computers improve at a task by finding patterns in data
neural network = a computing model loosely inspired by the brain, used in many AI systems
chatbot = a program that answers questions in written or spoken conversation
automation = using machines or software to do work with little human control
autonomous vehicle = a car or other vehicle that can drive itself in some or all conditions
AI bias = unfair results from an AI system because of skewed data or design
deepfake = a video or audio clip that uses AI to make someone appear to say or do things they did not
natural language processing = AI methods that let computers work with human speech and writing
facial recognition = technology that identifies people by analysing images of their faces
3D printing = making a solid object from a digital design, layer by layer
virtual reality = a computer-generated world experienced through a headset
augmented reality = technology that adds computer images or information to the real world you see
wearable technology = electronic devices designed to be worn, such as watches or fitness bands
humanoid robot = a robot built to look or move somewhat like a person
job displacement = workers losing posts because machines or software take over the tasks
dual-use technology = a tool or invention that can serve both civilian and harmful military purposes
voice assistant = software that answers spoken commands on a phone or speaker
general AI = a still-hypothetical system that could match or exceed human thinking across many tasks
genetic engineering = changing the genes of an organism in a planned way
genetically modified organism = a living thing whose DNA has been altered by genetic engineering
cloning = making a genetically identical copy of an organism or cell
genome = the complete set of genetic material of an organism
DNA sequencing = reading the order of chemical letters in a piece of DNA
stem-cell research = scientific work on cells that can develop into many types of body tissue
gene therapy = treatment that tries to cure disease by altering or replacing a gene
gene editing = precise techniques for changing DNA at a chosen place
designer baby = an informal name for a child whose genes have been chosen or changed before birth
space exploration = the investigation of space using telescopes, probes and crewed missions
spacecraft = a vehicle designed to travel in space
space station = a large structure in orbit where astronauts live and work
orbit = the curved path of an object around a planet or star
astronaut = a person trained to travel and work in space
telescope = an instrument that makes distant objects in space appear closer or clearer
black hole = a region in space with gravity so strong that not even light can escape
the Big Bang = the leading scientific explanation of how the universe began from an extremely hot, dense state
space probe = an uncrewed craft sent to study a planet, moon or other object
zero gravity = the floating condition in orbit where people and objects appear weightless
rocket launch = the event of sending a rocket from Earth into the sky or space
asteroid = a small rocky body that orbits the sun, mostly between Mars and Jupiter
Mars mission = a project to send a craft or people to Mars
space debris = dead satellites, fragments and other human-made junk in orbit
lunar landing = the arrival of a craft on the surface of the Moon
crewed mission = a space flight that carries people, not only instruments
extraterrestrial = coming from outside the Earth or its atmosphere
satellite launch = sending a satellite into orbit, usually on a rocket
screen addiction = an inability to control time spent on phones, games or social media despite harm
online misinformation = false or inaccurate information spread on the internet, often without the aim of causing harm
disinformation = false information created or shared on purpose to deceive
online echo chamber = an online space where you mainly see views you already agree with
filter bubble = personalised results that hide opposing information from you
data privacy = control over how your personal information is collected, stored and shared
surveillance = close watching of people, often with cameras or digital tracking
mass surveillance = watching large numbers of people, usually by a state or a huge platform
CCTV = cameras used to watch public or private spaces
identity fraud = using someone else’s personal details to steal money or services
cyberbullying = using digital messages or posts to frighten, shame or harass someone
clickbait headline = a title designed to make you open a page, often by exaggeration
doomscrolling = continuing to scroll through bad news even though it makes you feel worse
digital wellbeing = using technology in a way that protects mental health and attention
excessive screen use = spending so much time on phones or computers that sleep, school or health suffers
privacy settings = options that control who can see your information or activity
end-to-end encryption = a method in which only the sender and receiver can read a message, not the service in between
data protection law = legislation that limits how organisations may collect and use personal information
fact-checking = checking claims against reliable evidence before sharing them
viral content = a post or video that is shared by huge numbers of people in a short time
internet troll = a person who posts to upset, provoke or derail discussion
addictive design = product features meant to keep you using an app longer than you intended
online source evaluation = the skill of judging whether an online text is accurate, biased or fake
online harassment = repeated hostile behaviour towards someone through digital channels
location tracking = recording where a device, and therefore a person, goes
data mining = searching large sets of data for patterns, often for profit or prediction
biometric data = information from the body used to identify a person, such as a face, fingerprint or iris
smart grid = an electricity network that adjusts supply using digital data
fusion research = scientific work on joining atomic nuclei to produce energy
inventor = a person who creates a new device, process or product
scientific method = a way of testing ideas through observation, experiment and revision
researcher = a person whose job is to carry out systematic study in a field
laboratory = a room or building equipped for scientific experiments
open access = research papers that anyone can read without paying a subscription
quantum computer = a machine that uses quantum states to perform certain calculations far faster than ordinary computers
Internet of Things = everyday objects that connect to the internet and share data
5G network = a fifth-generation mobile network designed for higher speed and more devices
smart device = an electronic object that connects to a network and can be controlled by software
supercomputer = an extremely powerful computer used for complex scientific calculations
radio telescope = an instrument that collects radio waves from space rather than visible light
exoplanet = a planet that orbits a star other than the Sun
mission control = the ground centre that directs a space flight
particle accelerator = a machine that speeds up particles and smashes them together to study matter
metadata = data that describe other data, such as when a photo was taken or who sent an email
